# Troubleshooting

When the new-workspace wizard lists an existing Git repository, use Up/Down
and Space to select it, then Enter to confirm. **Add repository by path** is
for an explicitly supplied local Git root not in the immediate-child list; it
does not broaden discovery. Repository IDs are suggested from directory names
and are distinct from keyboard selection. A mistyped path can be corrected in
place. If branch/mapping validation fails, retry the repository mapping from
the same Control Workspace; no repository or installation files are changed
before approval.

Successful `npx triad-plus init --host opencode --control .` installs the
adapter assets only. It does **not** configure product-repository mappings,
quality gates, PRD, or worktrees. Check the project plan and readiness before
running `/triad`. When `doctor --control .` is run without `--host`, it
inspects all six adapters; `incomplete` for unused adapters is not evidence
that your chosen adapter is broken. Use `--host opencode` to inspect OpenCode
alone. Command errors are concise; run `npx triad-plus --help` for full syntax.

Run doctor first:

```bash
npx triad-plus doctor --host <runtime> --control /path/to/triad-control
```

Compare the executing CLI with the materialized workspace installation:

```bash
npx triad-plus --version
npx triad-plus version --control /path/to/triad-control
```

`legacy / manifest missing` means the workspace predates the installation
manifest. Run `upgrade --apply` to materialize a current manifest; Triad+ does
not infer the old version. The same `upgrade --apply` command is the managed
restore path after a safe uninstall leaves an `uninstalled` or `partial`
manifest: it re-materializes managed assets and reuses the preserved team
configuration and user state. `init` is reserved for first installation and
refuses existing paths. `manifest invalid` means the ownership record or its
fingerprint is malformed and should be reviewed before any uninstall.

Doctor also reports `CLI newer / upgrade available` and `CLI older than
installed version` instead of silently claiming compatibility. It never checks
the npm `latest` tag.

`not installed` means the selected adapter assets are absent from that control
workspace. `not installed or version unavailable` for a host means its binary is
not on PATH or otherwise cannot answer `--version`. Re-run the appropriate host
installer or fix the host environment; Triad+ does not require every runtime to
be present.

If a hook is unavailable, use explicit verification dispatch. Hooks are never a
requirement for a normal Triad run.

If a verifier result is `invalid_context`, compare the assignment, PRD/card/gate
baselines, worktree, branch, and candidate. Do not treat it as a passing test.

If Evaluator+ is unavailable, check `roles.evaluator.enabled` in the team file.
An Evaluator+ failure is post-run information, not an automatic repair request.

## Codex and Hermes entry bridge

The optional `$triad` Codex skill and Hermes `/triad` wrapper invoke an installed
built-ins-only global preflight before the local validator. Setup writes a
workspace-specific binding only after the owner approves the exact preview;
the binding pins the canonical Control Workspace, local manifest, and expected
project/global runtime hashes. A self-authored local manifest alone is not
trusted. The preflight checks the current directory and runs a temporary
snapshot of the verified validator, so a changed local validator is not
executed. A `BLOCKED` result means Triad has not started; there is no workspace
search or delegated work. Open/restart the host from the exact bound workspace
or approve setup from the desired workspace. This remains post-LLM; neither
skill can enforce a pre-LLM host boundary.

The Codex skill is installed at
`$CODEX_HOME/skills/triad/SKILL.md`. The former
`$CODEX_HOME/prompts/triad.md` custom prompt is left byte-for-byte untouched and
is not automatically migrated. If it exists, the wizard reports the collision
and blocks the optional Codex skill entry; back it up under another name or
skip the global Codex entry, then retry.

The guard also stops on an invalid installation manifest or asset hash,
missing/unsafe local adapter files, empty PRD, invalid quality gates, or missing
declared repository/worktree Git roots. Correct those inputs deliberately and
rerun; it does not infer or initialize them.

## Safe uninstall

Uninstall is a dry run unless `--apply` is supplied:

```bash
npx triad-plus uninstall --host <runtime> --control /path/to/triad-control
npx triad-plus uninstall --host <runtime> --control /path/to/triad-control --apply
```

Only unchanged files listed in `.triad-plus/installation.json` are removed.
`ABSENT` files are harmless. A `PRESERVE` line means the file was modified, no
longer matches the trusted managed plan, or is not a regular file; no force
option exists for this operation. Add `--global` only when user-level Triad
assets should also be considered. Global assets are nevertheless preserved by
default because another workspace may share them. Team config, loop state,
cards, artifacts, evidence, generic host directories, and other user files are
preserved. A managed `AGENTS.md` block is removed only when its exact markers
and hash still match; a modified or ambiguous block leaves the uninstall
partial. `version` and `uninstall` reject nonexistent control paths without
creating them.

## First increment: loadable model assets

`team.json` remains canonical **requested intent**. Managed model/effort
overrides are omitted from generated native files for all hosts; the legacy
Codex profile writer also omits them. Managed frontmatter upgrade removes stale
overrides and preserves intent. The current consented Codex entry installs a
skill/wrapper, not role profiles: existing user-level TOML files outside that
managed scope remain untouched and require separately previewed remediation. Setup summaries say requested
versus host default; an ID is never claimed selected merely because it is saved.
Lexical wizard checks reject spaces/control characters, require OpenCode's
`provider/model` shape, and stop after three invalid attempts without applying
the installation. These checks do not verify a model catalog.

Native model selection remains the host's responsibility and must be confirmed
or explicitly reported unobservable. The shared readiness/confirmation flow,
receipts and entry automation failures remain subsequent acceptance criteria;
the first increment does not claim them.

## Second increment: inactive gate proposals

Setup now prepares a per-repository/worktree inactive draft, with source hashes,
conservative npm-script candidates and prerequisite/context limitations.
Inspection and structure-only lint run no commands; explicit refresh replaces
only the draft. A correctly hashed inactive proposal is rejected by the verifier.
See [quality-gate discovery](quality-gate-discovery.md) for the data contract,
limits and controlled six-adapter/PTY evidence. Entry-time confirmation,
remediation, persisted readiness and complete native E2E remain pending.

## Gate boundary to preserve

The deterministic verifier runs gates in the assigned repository's worktree
and binds their source hash. Existing `assignment.gates_path` supports a
repository-specific catalog. Discovery must be read-only and proposals inactive;
it must not collect commands from several repositories into a catalog that runs
them all in one worktree. Manifest text is data, never agent instructions.
No discovered command, package lifecycle hook, install, publish, deploy,
Docker or VRT command may run merely to establish readiness.

# Guided workspace readiness

The six native entries now require the same preflight before loop planning,
bootstrap or delegation. Terminal use is also available:

```bash
npx triad-plus preflight --host opencode --control /absolute/control-workspace
npx triad-plus preflight --host opencode --control /absolute/control-workspace --non-interactive --json
```

The runtime entry also defaults to this consent-aware flow. Its explicit
`--structural-only` diagnostic never prints READY and is not authorization to
start the loop.

Use the exact Control Workspace and select the host explicitly. Interactive
mode guides one correction at a time. Without a terminal, or with
`--non-interactive`/`--json`, it never prompts or grants consent: unresolved
actions return exit 2. READY returns 0. Unchanged confirmed inputs need no
repeated questions or writes. A prompt has a two-minute timeout, invalid
choices have three attempts, and the overall pass is finite. Earlier completed
confirmations survive cancellation; an incomplete step does not grant consent.

## What READY means

Preflight validates installation/adapter compatibility and managed bytes,
canonical workspace paths, a nonempty root PRD, repository mappings and Git
baselines, existing base branches, separate worktrees and exact project
branches. It distinguishes fatal installation/configuration problems,
fixable owner actions and advisories. It does not invent PRDs, change branches,
create worktrees, install dependencies, run discovered commands or modify
external repositories. Dependency directory/executable presence checks are not
proof that arbitrary project tools or code work.

READY means current workspace bindings and explicit confirmations are valid.
It does **not** attest native host availability, provider credentials, effective
model identity, per-role model selection, script safety or a passing gate.
The deterministic verifier still produces execution evidence independently of
Reviewer reports. A host requiring an exact unavailable/unobservable model
must remain blocked unless the owner explicitly accepts the stated defaults.

## Models and host capabilities

`team.json` retains requested intent. Model syntax is checked without guessing
a replacement or claiming catalog availability. Correct one field with a
current-state-bound operation, or explicitly choose host defaults. Correction
does not materialize native overrides. Host-default consent preserves the
requests while recording that they are unapplied and identity is unobservable.
Optional Evaluator+ remains disabled unless configured explicitly.

| Host | Entry/preflight surface | Verifiable model/capability limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OpenCode | `/triad` and the Orchestrator profile run the common preflight | Use the project `/models` picker; syntax-valid is not available, and per-role overrides remain unapplied |
| Claude Code | `/triad` runs the common preflight | Session and subagent model controls differ; no shared catalog or portable effort translation is assumed |
| Codex | `$triad` runs its owner-bound global wrapper and trusted runtime snapshot | Global profile writes need separate exact-path consent; this increment does not verify/apply requested role models |
| GitHub Copilot | Skill and explicit Orchestrator agent fallback | CLI/IDE/cloud tool and prompt capabilities differ; disclose missing capabilities and use the owner terminal route |
| Antigravity | Skill and Orchestrator profile | Effective per-role model identity is not observable through this adapter |
| Hermes | Active-profile skill and owner-bound global wrapper | Use the exact trusted active-profile wrapper; CLI presence is not a working session and an unknown profile path is a blocker |

These entries are **model-instructed and post-LLM**, not enforced pre-LLM host
hooks. Generated agents remain loadable because they omit unverified model
overrides. If the host cannot run shell tools or prompt the owner, it must
disclose that limit and request the explicit terminal route rather than invent
READY. The complete native harness E2E and requested per-role model routing
remain release acceptance criteria; this increment does not complete them.

## Gate consent for one repository

The saved discovery draft is never trusted as an approval. Preflight reads the
current worktree, verifies its repository/branch identity and re-hashes known
manifest/lock sources. It shows candidate commands, their hashes, timeouts,
prerequisites and limits. Scripts and referenced project code are arbitrary
code: inspect their bodies locally before consent. Manifest bodies are never
emitted as agent instructions. `npm --ignore-scripts` is not a safety certificate.

Choose explicit candidate IDs, edit/provide a workspace-relative manual catalog,
or reject the proposal. Rejected unchanged candidates do not prompt again;
readiness remains blocked until the owner explicitly reopens or replaces that
choice. Manual catalogs are reviewed locally and their exact bytes are staged
before consent. Catalog lint proves structure only, not safety or tool identity.

For automation or a native conversational prompt, inspect first and use the
current report's `state_sha256` for **one** explicit owner-approved action:

```bash
# Read only. Replace the placeholders below from this current report.
npx triad-plus preflight --host opencode --control . --non-interactive --json
npx triad-plus preflight --host opencode --control . --approve models --expected-state <current-sha256>

# Inspect again after each step. Approve the first current gate action only.
npx triad-plus preflight --host opencode --control . --approve gates:backend --select test,lint --timeout 600 --expected-state <current-sha256>

# Stage/review a manual catalog before approving it; use its resulting state.
npx triad-plus preflight --host opencode --control . --catalog .loop/gates/backend.json --non-interactive --json
npx triad-plus preflight --host opencode --control . --catalog .loop/gates/backend.json --approve gates:backend --expected-state <current-sha256>

# Reopen a rejected or previously approved choice only at the owner's request.
npx triad-plus preflight --host opencode --control . --review gates:backend --non-interactive --json

# Correct intent without applying a native model. Blank after = clears it.
npx triad-plus preflight --host opencode --control . --set-model developer=provider/model --expected-state <current-sha256>
```

Until all steps are complete an approval can succeed while readiness still
returns exit 2; inspect the next action. Do not blindly retry or auto-approve.
Changed state/source/catalog bytes invalidate an old approval request before
writes. A selected proposal becomes a content-addressed catalog under
`.loop/gates/`; existing files are never overwritten. A manual catalog remains
at its explicitly approved path. `.loop/quality-gates.yaml` is preserved.

## Receipt, dispatch and verification

`.triad-plus/readiness.json` records confirmations for host defaults,
prerequisites and each repository's catalog. It binds current manifest source
hashes, canonical repository/worktree identity, branch and exact catalog bytes.
It records explicit CLI approval, not a cryptographic proof of human identity;
the Control Workspace remains owner-controlled configuration. Agents must not
forge receipts or infer consent.

Use the READY report's per-repository `gates_path` and
`expected_gates_sha256` when creating each immutable assignment. The shared
assignment resolver, used before dispatch and by the verifier, independently
checks current consent, source, branch/worktree and catalog bytes. A caller hash
or Reviewer verdict cannot substitute for that binding. Missing/deleted consent
blocks newly installed workspaces. Legacy standalone verifier fixtures without
an installed onboarding runtime retain their existing manual-catalog contract.

The independent guard also requires current global prerequisite consent: a safe,
non-empty root PRD with the confirmed hash and the current fingerprints of all
mapped repositories. Removing that confirmation, changing the PRD or changing
another mapped repository blocks new dispatch even if this assignment's catalog
consent is unchanged. Inspect readiness and explicitly reconfirm prerequisites
after review; this does not rewrite existing per-repository catalog approvals.
This global check does not attest per-host model/default consent or effective
model routing; those remain the native entry preflight's disclosed boundary.

Do not combine repositories into a catalog executed in one worktree. Do not
overwrite approved catalogs during bootstrap or mutate an existing assignment
to adopt a new approval. Gate/source/branch changes require fresh consent and
the normal new-attempt boundary. No run record, frozen PRD or old evidence is
rewritten by preflight.

## Existing global entries and remaining release limits

Codex/Hermes wrappers still verify owner-bound paths and bytes before running
local code; scoped approvals use that same temporary trusted snapshot. After
a project/runtime upgrade an older global binding can stop for byte drift.
Do not patch hashes or bypass it with changed local code. The installer preserves
shared global files on removal. For a current, package-matching project install,
use the separately consented [global entry refresh](global-entry-refresh.md):
preview exact existing paths, then apply with the current state hash. Old
multi-adapter installations requiring coordinated shared project upgrades remain
a limitation. The trusted package terminal route for workspace configuration
alone is not proof that a stale native global entry was repaired.

Evidence here is six-adapter contract coverage, actual terminal error → model
correction → READY, current-source/catalog/branch adversarial cases, and trusted
wrapper fixtures. These are not six native model sessions. The v1.22.4 release
acceptance adds one live OpenCode 1.19.3 host-default task; the other hosts and
per-role model routing remain unverified. Consent and deterministic verification
remain separate from model identity. See [release scope](releases/1.22.4.md).

# Verification and evidence

## Repository skill bindings

When a target repository declares a skill router, the Orchestrator binds the
router, routed task skills, and completion skill to the Developer assignment as
worktree-relative paths and SHA-256 values. `triad-verify` checks that every
declared skill exists inside the declared worktree and still matches its bound
hash, then records the result in environment-derived verification evidence.

This proves the exact repository skill policy available to the attempt; it does
not claim to observe an LLM's private reasoning. Developer, Reviewer, and
Evaluator+ must separately report their use of the same bound skills, so a
missing or inconsistent attestation is visible to the Orchestrator.

The Reviewer also returns a bounded `skill_compliance` list in its structured
result when repository skills are bound. Each entry names one bound skill path,
the compact rule locator evaluated, a `compliant`, `violated`, or
`not_applicable` status, and optional evidence references. An approved result
must cover every bound skill exactly once and cannot contain a violation. This
semantic attestation complements, and does not replace, the verifier's
path/SHA-256 identity check.

An agent-reported claim is not the same as verification evidence. A Developer can
report the commands it ran; `triad-verify` independently observes declared
required `control-plane` gates and writes atomic evidence.

## Explicit verifier dispatch contract

When the configured route is `explicit_dispatch`, invoke the installed verifier
with the active assignment's exact Developer identity. The trigger is supplied
as JSON on stdin; it is not inferred from the shell process or from the card:

```bash
agent_id="<assignment.agent_id>"
run_id="<assignment.verification_run_id>"
printf '{"event":"manual_explicit_dispatch","agent_id":"%s","agent_type":"triad_developer","run_id":"%s"}' "$agent_id" "$run_id" |
  node .triad-runtime/triad-verify.mjs \
    --project /absolute/path/to/control-workspace \
    --assignment /absolute/path/to/control-workspace/.loop/runtime/assignments/<assignment-file>.json \
    --run-id "$run_id"
```

`agent_id` must match the active assignment exactly and `agent_type` must be
`triad_developer`. The `run_id` on stdin and `--run-id` must match the active
assignment when one is bound. A missing or mismatched trigger is
`invalid_context`; no gate runs and no retry/remediation budget is consumed.

When the repository has no router or required repository skills, omit the
`required_repository_skills` property from the assignment. Do not represent an
unconfigured binding as a present empty array: a present array is a declared
binding and must contain at least one validated skill. This documents existing
runtime behavior; it does not add a new verifier mode or transition.

`triad-verify.mjs` does not expose a help screen. Use the assignment, project
configuration, and this explicit recipe rather than invoking it with `--help`.

## Immutable Quality Contract

Projects may opt into `project.quality_contract` with a project-relative JSON
manifest and its expected SHA-256 fingerprint. The shared
`runtime/lib/quality-baseline.mjs` loader canonicalizes the manifest (excluding
its self-declared `fingerprint`), validates source paths, IDs, scopes, and hashes,
then verifies every bound source before any expensive gate runs. A malformed,
missing, or mismatched contract is `invalid_context`; a valid manifest whose
bound source content has changed is `quality_baseline_drift`. Both fail closed:
no Developer dispatch, gate execution, or retry budget consumption is allowed.

The verifier records `baseline.quality_baseline_fingerprint` when configured and
records `null` for legacy projects. The Quality Contract is distinct from the
repository/card baseline and the candidate fingerprint: it says what the run is
trying to satisfy, not which Git commit was checked out or what the candidate
changed.

Before gates run, the verifier validates the active assignment, PRD/card/gate
hashes, worktree, expected branch, and candidate fingerprint. It records the
assignment ID/hash and run ID, executes deterministic commands with a bounded
timeout, and invalidates evidence if the candidate changes while gates run.

Only `control-plane` gate executors are supported in v1. A required unsupported
executor fails closed. Verifier evidence informs the Reviewer and Orchestrator;
it does not itself approve, rework, or transition a run.

Evidence files and logs are diagnostics. Users normally need only the
Orchestrator's summary and the Reviewer verdict.

## Workspace versus host authority

Triad delegates a product worktree, not the host. Roles may perform read-only
host diagnostics and run commands explicitly declared by the assignment or
trusted gate catalog. A process-local environment override is diagnostic only;
it is never canonical project configuration. Changing canonical executables or
toolchains, persistent PATH/profile files, `xcode-select` or license state,
global packages/symlinks/configuration, permissions outside the assigned
workspace, credentials/accounts, daemons/services, or publish/tag/release state
requires explicit owner authorization unless the exact action was declared by
the run. This boundary is independent of the adapter and does not pretend to
provide OS-level sandboxing.

For each control-plane gate, Triad records declared command and cwd plus a
best-effort direct-executable provenance snapshot (resolved absolute path,
binary SHA-256, and version when available). Composite shell commands are
explicitly recorded as `unresolved_shell_command` rather than parsed. A gate
may opt into a trusted `toolchain` binding (`executable`, `sha256`, and/or
`version`); a mismatch or an unresolvable bound executable fails closed before
any gate command runs. Legacy gates without a binding continue to run and are
recorded as unbound; no environment variables or secrets are copied into
evidence.

## Assignment packets and dispatch context

The Orchestrator can create one immutable packet per active assignment with:

```bash
node .triad-runtime/triad-assignment-packet.mjs \
  --project /absolute/path/to/control-workspace \
  --assignment .loop/runtime/assignments/<assignment-file>.json
```

The command binds a packet path and SHA-256 to the assignment and returns the
explicit product-worktree `dispatch.cwd`. The packet contains the bounded card
contract, relevant excerpts, verification mapping, expected paths, risks,
constraints, mandatory skill references, and prior evidence references. It is
the primary Developer/Reviewer context; full PRD/ADR reads are fallback-only.
It never replaces real skill reads or verifier hash checks. A bound packet is
validated before `triad-verify` executes scope or gates, and a changed or
missing packet fails closed as `assignment_packet_invalid`. Assignments without
packet fields retain legacy behavior.

## Optional generic evidence manifest

An assignment may opt into one repository-owned evidence manifest by binding
both `evidence_directory` and `evidence_manifest_path`. The manifest is a
generic JSON record of bounded artifact metadata; it is not a browser, domain,
or artifact-management subsystem. Its artifact paths are resolved only inside
the explicit evidence directory and every artifact must be a regular file with
the declared SHA-256 and byte length. The verifier also requires the manifest
to match the active run, assignment, feature, attempt, producer gate, and
pre-gate candidate fingerprint.

The repository-owned gate creates the manifest and artifacts. `triad-verify`
validates them after the declared gates and records compact `artifact_manifest`
metadata in verification evidence. Missing, stale, tampered, out-of-root,
traversal, symlink, or non-regular artifacts fail closed as
`evidence_manifest_invalid`; a Reviewer is not dispatched. Assignments without
`evidence_manifest_path` take the unchanged legacy path. Binary contents are
not copied into role prompts; the Reviewer remains the semantic judge of any
accepted reference.

## Card-declared required gates

The work queue may carry a machine-readable `required_gates` list for an
individual card. The values are repository-owned gate IDs; Triad does not infer
their purpose or know whether a gate checks UI, an API, a migration, or another
concern.

An absent or empty list preserves the v1.5 legacy execution behavior. When the
list is non-empty, the Orchestrator resolves one effective set by taking the
union of every trusted repository gate whose definition has `required: true`
and the card-selected IDs. The set is deduplicated. A selected optional gate is
promoted to required for that card, while unselected optional gates may be
skipped. The trusted catalog remains authoritative for command, timeout, and
executor details.

Every selected ID is validated before Developer dispatch. A missing ID,
placeholder command, or unsupported executor is an
`unavailable_required_gate` capability gap: the Developer is not dispatched and
no retry budget is consumed. The verifier repeats the binding check so a stale
assignment fails closed. Verification evidence records the mode, card-selected
IDs, baseline required IDs, effective IDs, and effective required IDs. A verifier
pass still always leads to an independent Reviewer; gate pass is not semantic
approval.

## Optional deterministic candidate scope

Cards may add a versioned JSON scope contract, bound by path and SHA-256 in the
Developer assignment. The contract names repository-relative `allowed_paths`,
optional `allowed_incidental_paths`, and `forbidden_paths` for each target
repository. It uses a small glob syntax: `*` does not cross a directory,
`**` may cross directories, and `?` matches one non-separator character.

For a scope-bound card, the Orchestrator captures a clean card baseline commit
before the first assignment and reuses it for every rework attempt. The verifier
compares the full cumulative candidate delta against that baseline before running
expensive gates. It records changed paths and offending paths in evidence. A
scope failure skips expensive gates and Reviewer dispatch; it is bounded
`scope_cleanup`, not approval. A card without a scope contract records
`scope_not_configured` and retains legacy behavior.

Package manifests and lockfiles require an explicit `allowed_incidental_paths`
entry. Snapshot patterns must be narrow; broad `snapshots/**` contracts are
rejected. A scope pass is only a deterministic path check: Reviewer remains
mandatory for semantic scope, correctness, design, and risk.

## Codex dispatch modes

Codex uses `explicit_dispatch` by default, including when a compatible async
`SubagentStop` hook is installed. This is the directly auditable path used for
normal unattended progress. The async hook remains supported as an experimental
opt-in with `requested_mode=async_hook`; it is selected only when the requested
hook is valid and available. If that requested hook is unavailable, capability
detection fails safe to `explicit_dispatch` and records the reason.

Hooks may produce evidence; the Orchestrator governs progress. The hook never
dispatches a Reviewer, selects a card, reopens a run, or performs repair.

## Color and typography contract

| Role | Treatment | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Brand | Violet `#7C8CFF` + turquoise `#35C3B1`; amber `#F5B95E` for `+` | Identity, shown large once on entry and compact on later screens |

# GitHub Release to npm publishing

The release workflow publishes an already verified package only after a stable
GitHub Release has been published. It never creates a tag or Release, and a
failed or partially completed publication requires inspection rather than a
blind rerun.

## One-time npm Trusted Publisher setup

In npmjs.com settings for the existing `triad-plus` package, configure a
GitHub Actions Trusted Publisher with these exact, case-sensitive values:

- GitHub user/organization: `ainz-dg`
- Repository: `triad-plus-engineering-loop`
- Workflow filename: `release.yml` (filename only, not the
  `.github/workflows/` path)
- Environment: leave empty; the workflow does not use a GitHub Environment

The workflow uses Node 24 and pins npm to 11.5.1, which meets the npm Trusted
Publishing minimum. The `publish-npm` job alone receives `id-token: write`; the separate
Release-assets job alone receives `contents: write`. No npm token secret,
`NODE_AUTH_TOKEN`, or static-token fallback is used. Do not work around an OIDC
failure by adding a token.

npm requires a new Trusted Publisher configuration to complete its first
successful publish within two days. Configure it only when the owner is ready
to perform the first real release. The repository cannot inspect or prove the
account-side setting; it is verified only by a successful OIDC publication.

## Owner-controlled release procedure

1. Merge the reviewed release-preparation change only after an explicit owner
   GO and green checks on the exact merge commit.
2. Confirm `package.json` has the intended stable release version. The package
   version must equal the version in a canonical `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` tag.
3. Create and publish the stable GitHub Release from the GitHub UI, targeting
   the current `main` commit. The Release must be authored by `ainz-dg`, be
   neither draft nor prerelease, and its tag must resolve to the current
   `main` SHA. The workflow rejects ambiguous branch targets and moved tags.
4. Publishing the Release starts `.github/workflows/release.yml`. For a
   `release` event GitHub sets `GITHUB_REF` to `refs/tags/<tag>` and
   `GITHUB_SHA` to the last commit in that tagged release. The workflow checks
   both values, checks out that immutable SHA, resolves the remote tag and
   current `main`, and verifies the Release metadata again before npm writes.
   GitHub's `published` activity can include prereleases, so the workflow
   explicitly rejects those before publication.
5. Wait for all jobs to finish. The gate rebuilds and tests, runs the package
   checks and `prepublishOnly`, then creates one verified tarball and SHA-256
   sidecar. The `publish-npm` job ends after publishing that exact artifact
   with provenance; it does not repack. A separate `verify-npm` job checks
   registry propagation and the exact integrity/shasum. Only after that job
   succeeds may asset upload and final published checks proceed.
   The existing Release receives only the matching `.tgz` and
   `.tgz.sha256` assets, and the final job verifies their API digests and
   downloaded bytes plus a registry install smoke test.

`workflow_dispatch` is a side-effect-free gate/build run on the exact current
`main` SHA. It has no publish mode and does not upload an artifact, publish to
npm, or modify a Release or tag. It rejects versions, tags, or Releases that
already exist. It cannot prove that npm OIDC is configured or simulate an OIDC
exchange. Do not use the previously recovered `v1.22.1` as a trigger test.

## Fail-closed behavior and recovery

- Only `release` with action `published` or the read-only dispatch path is
  accepted. Stable tag syntax, actor, package name/version, release metadata,
  tag SHA, target commit, checked-out commit, and current `main` must agree.
- An existing npm version, tag, or Release is a conflict. A tag is never moved;
  an immutable npm version is never replaced. Registry errors other than a
  confirmed E404 fail closed.
- npm propagation uses a ten-minute time budget, checking every 15 seconds
  only while the exact version is temporarily absent (confirmed E404/No match).
  Probe latency consumes the budget; npm internal fetch retries are disabled
  and each request has at most 30 seconds or the remaining budget.
  `REGISTRY_BUDGET_MS` (1..600000) and `REGISTRY_DELAY_MS` (1..budget) allow
  shorter controlled checks in `verify-registry`. A visible version with the
  wrong `dist.integrity` or
  `dist.shasum`, or any non-404 registry error, stops immediately. A timeout
  reports `WAITING/NOT YET VISIBLE` and fails; it never falls back to publish.
  `npm view --prefer-online` forces cache freshness checks
  ([npm config](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/using-npm/config/#prefer-online)).
  No evidence requires a costly cache purge, so recovery does not clear it.
- The GitHub Release is already public before npm publication begins. This is
  deliberately non-atomic: if npm rejects OIDC or a later job fails, the
  public Release remains. The workflow does not create a second Release or tag.
- Existing Release assets are never overwritten. Missing expected assets may
  be uploaded only after npm succeeds; unexpected assets or digest conflicts
  stop the job. If npm accepted the package but a later step failed, do not
  rerun publication. Use the standalone verification procedure below. Stop for
  owner review on any mismatch; never republish or move a tag.
- A Release created by a workflow using `GITHUB_TOKEN` generally will not
  trigger another workflow. Publish the owner-approved Release through the
  GitHub UI so this workflow receives the normal `published` event.

## Verification-only recovery after npm accepted a version

**Rerunning all, failed, or individual jobs in `release.yml` is forbidden for
recovery after npm accepted a version.** This includes `verify-npm` and
`gh run rerun --job`: dependency/rerun behavior is not a recovery contract.
Use only `.github/workflows/release-recovery.yml`, after its reviewed code has
landed on `main`. It has `contents: read` and `actions: read`, no OIDC grant,
no npm credentials, no package writes, and no dependency on a publisher.
It never rebuilds, repacks, installs, uploads, or overwrites anything remotely.

For the historical propagation failure, the exact approved inputs are:

```sh
gh workflow run release-recovery.yml \
  --repo ainz-dg/triad-plus-engineering-loop --ref main \
  -f release_tag=v1.22.3 \
  -f expected_commit=7327d8df957931e07d6ba76305f2f27e4dffe76c \
  -f original_run_id=42388541647
```

Only `ainz-dg` may dispatch from canonical `main`. Supply a stable tag, full
lowercase release SHA and original run ID; hashes are never caller inputs.
The recovery script executes from the dispatch SHA, checks the historical
commit is in `origin/main`, and never executes historical source or package
code. Unlike publication, recovery allows `main` to have advanced.

Identity is bound to GitHub's authenticated read APIs: the original completed
`release.yml` release run, repository, owner, tag, SHA and first attempt must
agree. The original gate and publish preflight must have succeeded, as must
the exact `npm publish` step (even when its containing historical job failed).
The current stable Release must be owner-authored, target `main` or the exact
SHA, and have been published no later than the original run; the remote tag
must still resolve to that SHA. This rejects a later replacement Release.

The original gate logs must identify the exact immutable artifact ID and ZIP
SHA-256. The artifact API must bind it to the source run/repository/SHA/tag;
its downloaded ZIP is hashed locally and must match both the API and those
logs. Only the original archive and SHA-256 sidecar are accepted. The gate's
archive digest and the successful publisher's logged expected SHA-256,
sidecar SHA-256, SHA-512 integrity and SHA-1 shasum must all match the actual
bytes. The archive's package identity is read without installing it.
Existing Release assets must match API digests **and** downloaded bytes.
Registry `version`, `dist.integrity` and `dist.shasum` are compared with the
original archive, never regenerated bytes or caller assertions.

This is checksummed evidence, not a newly signed release or a replacement for
npm provenance. Its trust boundary includes GitHub's API/log/artifact storage,
reviewed code on `main`, and the authorized repository owner. Artifact digest
metadata is documented by [GitHub's artifact API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/actions/artifacts).
Missing/expired artifacts, deleted logs, missing hashes, conflicting evidence,
a rerun source (`run_attempt != 1`), incomplete API results, or any unexpected
npm error are `BLOCKED/MISMATCH`; there is no fallback to Release downloads,
registry tarballs, rebuilding, or publishing. Formats changed by upstream
GitHub/npm may also require a separately reviewed verifier update.

Results appear in logs and the Actions summary:

- `VERIFIED`: registry identity matches the original exact archive. The report
  also lists missing Release assets; verified npm does not imply assets exist.
- `WAITING/NOT YET VISIBLE`: only temporary E404/No match; bounded expiry fails
  the recovery run. A later invocation of **this workflow** is safe.
- `BLOCKED/MISMATCH`: stop for owner inspection; no further recovery writes.

The historical v1.22.3 run remains **failed**. A successful new verification
neither changes that conclusion nor modifies the old run, tag, Release,
artifact, or npm version. Repeating verification cannot publish a second copy.

## Separately authorized manual asset recovery

Missing assets require separate owner authorization. After a successful
verification, an authorized maintainer may download the **same original run
artifact ID**, validate its ZIP and all byte hashes against the original logs,
and upload only the names reported missing. For example, after inspecting
those original bytes (not after repacking):

```sh
# Run only with separate owner authorization, from the verified artifact directory.
# Omit either path if that asset already exists. Never add --clobber.
gh release upload v1.22.3 \
  ./triad-plus-1.22.3.tgz ./triad-plus-1.22.3.tgz.sha256 \
  --repo ainz-dg/triad-plus-engineering-loop
```

Recheck Release ID, tag SHA and existing asset digests immediately before the
upload. Stop on any conflict; do not replace assets. Download and hash the
resulting assets, then repeat the standalone verification. This manual path
is outside the read-only workflow and does not make the historical run green.

## Scope

This workflow is not a general CI trigger: it has no push, pull-request, or
schedule publishing path, no auto-merge, and no tag or Release creation. It
does not change Triad+ runtime behavior. A published Release is the explicit
owner-controlled authorization point; the final npm write remains guarded by
the exact verified artifact and npm OIDC.

# Triad+ 1.19.0

**Status:** Published on 2026-10-17 (Europe/Rome) to npm and as a GitHub
Release. This page records the released package and its verified limits.

**Package:** [`triad-plus@1.19.0`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/triad-plus/v/1.19.0)

**GitHub Release:** [v1.19.0](https://github.com/ainz-dg/triad-plus-engineering-loop/releases/tag/v1.19.0)

**Released commit:** `f3833e071fe03c5396babc3117529987368522e3` (`main` and
`v1.19.0` resolve to this commit).

## Summary

This release updates the terminal first-run experience for selecting a
Control Workspace, explicitly mapping product repositories, and installing
one or more registered adapters in a reviewed setup plan. It also records an
integrated local-only smoke for selecting and installing all six adapters in
one pseudo-terminal session. The release delta also adds path- and
assignment-bound visibility for assigned attempt evidence in the read-only
Cockpit and refreshes the OpenCode quickstart for separate control and product
repositories.

This is onboarding and installation inventory work. It does not add new Core
behavior, host-native discovery, or per-Attempt adapter selection or dispatch.
Installing multiple adapters does not route an Attempt between harnesses.

## New-workspace onboarding

Running `npx triad-plus` without a registered installation in the current
directory defaults to **New workspace**; a valid manifest defaults to
**Manage existing**. The wizard does not search sibling directories. For new
setup it asks for a separate Control Workspace root. A Control Workspace can
be non-Git while mapped product repositories are independent Git roots; a
Control Workspace inside a Git root is refused rather than repurposing or
migrating that repository.

Repository mapping is an explicit choice:

- **Existing:** select local Git repositories and declare each ID, path, base
  branch, project branch, and worktree. Read-only immediate-child suggestions
  are not selected automatically.
- **Greenfield:** select empty paths to initialize as local Git repositories
  only after approval. No remote is created and nothing is pushed.
- **Defer:** skip mappings; setup may install assets but remains **NOT READY**
  until the required repository and project inputs exist.

The wizard does not clone from a URL or search sibling directories. It can
select several of the six registered adapters in one session. An optional
team identity/model configuration may also be requested. A preview names the
exact Control Workspace, repository mapping, project-local files, and
readiness result. Only the exact `install` confirmation applies that plan.
Global/user-level host files, credentials, and account settings are not
written.

The preview is read-only. Unsafe paths, a Control Workspace under a product
Git root, or preflight conflicts stop setup. Relevant root, role-configuration,
mapping, ownership, and collision conditions are checked before or during
application; changed inputs are not silently overwritten. If a later adapter
installation fails, earlier successful steps are retained and reported rather
than automatically deleted; inspect the partial installation before retrying.
This is not a transactional rollback.

Installation does not establish Triad readiness. The post-setup readiness
check reports missing root `PRD.md`, `.loop/quality-gates.yaml`, initial Git
commits, and mapped worktrees; setup does not create these implicitly. In
particular, a greenfield `git init` is not an initial baseline commit.

## Existing-workspace management and scriptable CLI

An already registered workspace follows the management path rather than
first-run onboarding. The wizard offers list, add, doctor/status, upgrade,
remove, and exit. `init` refuses to overwrite a registered installation;
`upgrade --apply` is the managed update/repair path for an existing workspace.
Existing scripts can continue to use the CLI commands, including
`init`, `adapter add`, `doctor`, `version`, `upgrade`, and
`uninstall`; the terminal wizard does not replace those interfaces.

The schema-v2 adapter inventory records project-local membership and managed
asset ownership. It does not select a host for an Attempt, provide
per-Attempt multi-harness dispatch, or imply that a host can discover or invoke
the installed files. The read-only Cockpit can expose assigned attempt
verification documents only after their declared attempt path and
assignment/evidence identity bindings validate; this does not open general
filesystem access to arbitrary evidence paths.

## Package and verification boundaries

The release requires Node.js **>=20** and declares **zero runtime
dependencies**. The first-install smoke used a non-Git Control Workspace and a
separate direct-child Git repository, selected all six adapters in one TUI
session, approved one project-only installation plan, and checked the
schema-v2 manifest plus read-only `adapter list` and `adapter doctor`
results. This is a local artifact/install smoke, not six native-host tests.

**Native discovery and invocation are NOT VERIFIED** for the installed host
entries. In particular, the current evidence does not establish the Codex
user-level prompt contract from this non-Git Control Workspace or a Hermes
entry installed in a user profile. The local-only smoke intentionally made no
global writes. Adapter presence is not evidence of native host recognition.

Attempt-bound multi-harness dispatch is **NOT SUPPORTED**. No claim is made
that an Attempt can choose or route to a harness based on this installation.
M1B traceability remains a separate audit stream. Ketchup2 benchmark work
remains stopped for leakage review and is outside this release.

The release package smoke verified the published npm artifact and the published
GitHub tag was resolved to the same commit shown above. These checks confirm
publication identity; they do not expand the feature or host-compatibility
claims in this document.

- **Post-run PR planning.** The opt-in `triad-pr-plan` flow supports deterministic grouping, canonical dependency checks, byte-bound plans, explicit owner approval, drift checks, and draft-only PR creation. It does not generate source snapshots or schedule draft creation in-loop. Operators must prepare the approved snapshots and group worktrees, branches, and pushes. Automatic stacked PRs, merging, and cost reduction are not claimed.
- **Pre-run structure approval and multi-Card baselines.** The Orchestrator can obtain explicit approval for exact Card grouping and branch/worktree/base/remote bindings before implementation. Post-run verification refreshes canonical evidence; a Card's candidate check uses its own canonical baseline while group-level draft validation still requires the exact approved commits. Legacy post-run approval remains available.

# OpenCode: from a Control Workspace to your first reviewed result

This walkthrough connects setup, a first OpenCode-driven Triad+ loop, its
recorded evidence, the optional human-readable reports, and the read-only
Cockpit. It is a procedure, not a promise that a full loop finishes within a
fixed time.

For v1.22.4, a separate package-tarball acceptance completed one small native
OpenCode 1.19.3 task in host-default mode. The roles shared the same session
default; this does not verify per-role model/effort routing or other host
sessions. See [compatibility](../compatibility.md).

## Before you start

- Node.js 20 or newer and npm.
- OpenCode installed and configured on this machine, with a model available to
  the host. OpenCode's provider login and model setup are host prerequisites;
  Triad+ does not create credentials or prove which model a session used.
- A local Git product repository and a clear goal small enough to review.
- Permission to create a separate Control Workspace and a declared worktree.

Keep the Control Workspace outside the product repository. It stores the PRD,
work queue, assignments, verifier evidence, reports, and configuration; the
product repository remains the source of product code. A local mapping is not
a clone or a push.

## 1. Create and map the Control Workspace

Start from a new directory that is not inside the product repository:

```bash
mkdir -p "$HOME/projects/sample-control"
cd "$HOME/projects/sample-control"
npx triad-plus
```

In the wizard, choose **New workspace**, keep this separate directory as the
Control Workspace, map the existing local product repository, declare its base
and project branches plus worktree, and select **OpenCode**. The concise
confirmation can be expanded with `details`; exact-path review is required
when a user-level entry is selected before confirming `install`. The wizard
does not create the product worktree, PRD, quality gates, or initial
product-repository commit. It does not log in to OpenCode or write global host
configuration unless an optional entry is selected and approved.

Check the installed version and host/installation diagnostics from the Control
Workspace:

```bash
npx triad-plus version --control .
npx triad-plus doctor --host opencode --control .
```

The setup preview is an installation plan; it does not inspect project
readiness or probe host availability. `doctor` separately diagnoses the
adapter, managed project assets, host executable, and available host/verifier
configuration; it does not establish project readiness or run quality gates.
A successful installation is not the same as a ready project. Check the
required project inputs separately before starting the loop.

## 2. Write the goal and deterministic quality gates

Create `PRD.md` at the Control Workspace root. State the desired outcome and
observable acceptance criteria; keep product requirements in the PRD rather
than embedding them in setup commands. Add `.loop/quality-gates.yaml` with
commands appropriate to the mapped product repository. For example, a Node
project might declare its real test script as a required gate:

```yaml
gates:
  - id: tests
    command: npm test
    required: true
```

Use the gate format and executor supported by the installed Triad+ version;
the example command is valid only when that product repository actually has
an `npm test` script. Commit the product baseline and create the worktree
declared in the project mapping. The setup wizard does none of those tasks.
The wizard does not create the PRD, gate commands, commits, or worktree. Use
the preview to resolve structural setup gaps and `doctor` for host or
installation issues. `triad-verify` later runs the declared gates for a
recorded Attempt.

## 3. Start the OpenCode loop

Open OpenCode with the Control Workspace as its working directory:

```bash
opencode
```

In the interactive session, start the installed command with the root PRD:

```text
/triad ./PRD.md
```

The Orchestrator selects a Card and directs the normal
Developer → verification → Reviewer path. OpenCode is the host that runs the
interactive workflow; `triad-verify` records environment-derived gate results.
The Cockpit is not part of execution and will not start agents. A persisted
`in_progress` declaration is not evidence that an agent is currently alive.

## 4. Follow the evidence, not just status words

The work queue is `.loop/work-queue.yaml`. Assignments and immutable packets
are under `.loop/runtime/assignments/`; attempt evidence is recorded below
`.loop/evidence/<card-id>/attempt-NNN/`. A passing verifier result is bound to
the candidate fingerprint and declared gates at the time it ran. It does not
re-run itself when the candidate later changes. Read it alongside the diff and
Reviewer record; a status written in YAML or prose is a declaration, not a
validated result. See [Verification and evidence](../verification.md) for the
provenance contract.

Triad+ does not create human-readable reports merely because a renderer is
installed. After a Card is terminal, the Orchestrator must explicitly invoke
the [report renderer](../human-readable-reports.md) with context derived from
the canonical Card, verification, and review records. That produces
`card-reports/<card-id>.md`; the final project handoff is materialized
separately as `handoff.md` when the delivery context is ready. A missing file
is simply unavailable—it is not an approval or a delivery failure.

## 5. Read the project and Card in Cockpit

After the workspace has project and Card data, run this in a terminal at the
Control Workspace root:

```bash
npx triad-plus cockpit
```

The current Control Workspace is validated automatically; pass
`--control <path>` to select a different one explicitly. A local interactive
desktop opens the one-time loopback link when safe, and the URL is always
printed as a fallback. Use `--no-open` to suppress automatic opening. The
server is local and read-only; `Ctrl+C` stops it. It reads persisted
artifacts and does not run a gate, start an agent, or materialize a report.

On the project view, **Delivery handoff** opens the existing `handoff.md` when
that file is available. Select a Card to see **Card report** separately from
the Verifier, Reviewer, and Evaluator+ signals. These signals have distinct
provenance: a declared Card state or Markdown statement is not elevated to a
verdict by being visible in Cockpit. Evaluator+ is optional after approval; it
is not a fourth Triad role or a repair controller. The viewer renders Markdown
as inert text, does not fetch links or images, and keeps wide tables and code
inside their own scroll areas on narrow viewports.

## When something is absent or blocked

- Use the setup preview for structural input/path gaps and `doctor` for host
  and installation diagnostics; neither creates missing inputs or runs gates.
- If no Card report or `handoff.md` exists, first check whether the relevant
  Card is terminal or whether the Orchestrator has invoked the renderer. The
  Cockpit will show the document as unavailable rather than generating it.
- If a gate fails or evidence is stale, use the recorded failure and current
  diff to decide the next step. Do not call an agent claim a passing gate.
- These screenshots and the Cockpit package smoke are not native-session
  evidence. The separate v1.22.4 acceptance records a live `/triad` package
  task on OpenCode 1.19.3 with a consented host default; adapter-file presence
  alone still does not prove a working host session.

For exact report-context fields, see [Human-readable reports](../human-readable-reports.md).
